blocks.x: Proof of the voice? No?

Well, yeah, we check. We'll check it now. She'll watch while we talk. We just talk naturally. Let's see, uh, can I get your name first just to check the... Okay. ...watch? Uh, is it picking him up okay? Say your name.
Joseph Balzerak.
Joseph Balzerak.
Oh, look at this. On the input it was doing fine.
Okay. What turned it up?
I did that.
More. Because it's just barely picking me up. You don't want to go over to the red. I know that. What's today's date? Today is, uh...
Uh, Friday.
17th of May.
May 17th?
May 17th, 1968. Yeah. New Orleans.
And your name?
My name? Alan Ellis.
Yeah, my name is Dick Allen. And we're going to talk about, uh, you a little bit. Do you mind if I ask, uh, when you were born and where you were born?
You want to know?
Yes.
I'm born in Warsaw. 1915. So I'm an old man, but not old-timer.
What is your birthday, exact day of birth? Where? What is your day that you were born in March?
March 7th. March 7th. Mm-hmm.
And, uh, did you hear any jazz when you were, uh, growing up as a child?

Of course. No, first time I have, uh, my first contact with jazz was after my school education. And my first job I got in Warsaw at the branch of American film company United Artists and London, London Films from London. Uh, as a clerk and then as a chief of publicity and press department, before of my previous experience in journalist life. Uh, and in my office, uh, exactly in the same department, uh, I had a friend, Jackie Rotvandowna, girl, uh, who was very interested in jazz life and make plenty of journeys to our European, uh, center in London. And every few weeks, every few months, she brought with, when she came back, plenty of records, jazz records. And then she invites musicians, including me as a friend from the same office, to private jam sessions. And, uh, and it was my first connections with this world. It was like, uh, uh, for me, like a hobby. And then I was very often, I've been in various clubs, restaurants, cafe, nightclubs, where Polish jazz musicians, now we call them old generation, of course, played jazz. Of course, as usual, as in the whole world, it was, uh, 30s. And jazz was half a music, uh, in half, uh, sense was a music for amusement, for dance. And partly for, uh, loving jazz, really pure jazz. It was not so, this border was not like today. And, uh, uh, was no enemies of, uh, this style or other style, because we knew only one jazz. Like Benny Goodman, uh, Duke Ellington, Teddy Wilson, and so on, and so on. And, uh, of course, uh, very popular in Poland, we, uh, had, uh, English groups. Nat Gonella, Jack Payne, I don't remember exactly now, uh, and other names. And, uh, in every music shop we have plenty of American and English records. Um, not the same situation we have, uh, today in Poland. Only from occasion to occasion we can hear these records. We cannot buy only from time to time, Polish state, um, record company, make exchange or something like that, but it is only by occasion. So it was my first steps to love music called jazz.
Mm-hmm. Did, how long did this last that you could listen to jazz? Was it interrupted? Stopped?

Um, it was very, very nice, uh, time until, uh, 38, because it was, uh, the time when comes clothes over Europe, and I began my military service, and that was the end of my music, um, interests. Of course, not, uh, exactly, uh, interest, but no possibility to hear except military music. As you can imagine, it is not the same. It was 38, uh, and very, I have very hard, uh, my military service before Hitler came to Poland. Poland, and only, uh, twice when I've been on a vaca-, not vacation, it is a special possibility to come home for one or two days.
Leave it.

Yes. Uh, immediately after, uh, immediately in the same evening I must to hear jazz music in nightclubs, because it was something like hunger. Everybody, everybody can understand such a situation. And then was interruption, uh, a few years of war. Uh, and I have very, uh, funny, uh, incident during the war. When I have been the second time in military, in 44 and 45, once, I've been in the Germany, um, before the end of the war, with the army. As you know, from one side, uh, Anglo-American army, and I was in the army, Polish army, that was together with the Russian army. And in one house, when we stopped for one night, I found a few German records, and one of these records was, uh, Benny Goodman group, and one record was Nelson Eddy and Janet MacDonald. But the cover of this record has a German, uh, print, uh, mark, with another names of, uh, composers, and names of, uh, compositions, and names of interpreters, uh, of, uh, musicians. Uh, of course, uh, German musicians. It was, uh, Haydn, um, it was this mark of, of record, was, uh, hidden or Haydn, how it is? Yes, hidden. Hidden. And only owner of this, uh, of, of this apartment that was not here in this moment, he is gone. Uh, only the owner, uh, knew about that, uh, mystification. And it was a very happy moment for me when I put this record, plenty of records on the gramophone, and we make this whole story true, that it is a jazz record and pop record from America, because American music was prohibited in Germany during Hitler, especially jazz, because they called jazz music of Negro, and Negro was the enemy of the race, pure race of Germans. So it is one of accident during the war. And next it is another story, maybe you have more questions.
Yes. Well, what happened after the war was over?

When war is over, I have been in the Navy, Polish Navy, as an editor of Navy magazine. And I have no special connections with music, few years until 1948. And in this time I have finished my military service and began to work in Radio Gdańsk. You know that in Gdańsk was the first shot of Second World War. It was very interesting work for me, because I have been employed in the Department of Reports from sailors' life and so on. And partly I was a collaborator of the Department of Music because of my interest in so-called jazz music. It was the time that jazz was not prohibited, but very popular was such music like George Gershwin, for instance. Very popular, very popular, and I made the first steps to making something like light music and jazz program at Gdańsk Radio. Then was very, for me personally, it was very hard to note that I have heard in this time that in Warsaw and in Krakow, our old capital, Polish capital, university town in South Park, that they have clubs organized from pre-war time by organization YMCA. And they have plenty of gramophone records and make something like jam sessions, partly from records, partly from live concerts with lectures. For instance, in Warsaw, I have Leopold Tiermann, our writer, fewer lectures, if I know, in Warsaw clubs. In Gdańsk we have only a small club and only from time to time I have this occasion. Then comes, beginning from 1948 until 1952, so until the death of Stalin, comes the times of silence of music, beginning from such kind of music, music, because it's called like music of Western, how it's called?
Say it in Polish.
Oh, I have here.
Do you have it here? Mm-hmm. You talked there about decadent capitalism, the capitalists of the UK. Yes, yes, something like that, it's called so. Decadent music and so on.

It was, of course, the same language like in Russia, because they didn't believe that it is also art, yes. And they told that all music that came from America, it is not a good music, so we can listen only Polish music, Russian music, and of course, our old composers from symphonic music and so on. That is the reason that it comes time for listening jazz only at home, on private meetings, in schools, and dancing, private dancing and so on. Non-official life of jazz. Mm-hm.
Mm-hm.

Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. became favorable to Jess. Little sparks sprung up here and there. Mysterious posters appeared on the walls of Warsaw announcing things like performances. Was extremely simple. Just some hole in the railway workers club. Leopold Thiermann, the former Habitue How do you pronounce it? Habitue? Habitue of the IMCA, who later was to become a well-known writer, arranged a series of concerts with the participation of enthusiastic groups from Warsaw, Krakow, Luch. The public throned the halls in crowds never seen before. Their favorites, except of American that can hear from records, became Polish musicians. Matuszkiewicz, sax clarinet, Walasek, sax tenor, Sobocinski drums, Wojciechowski trumpet, Kujawski bass, Guziński trumpet, Trzaskowski and Kurilewicz piano, Byliński drums and Jean Johnston, the rediscovered vocalist of the AMCA days, British wife of the Polish pilot. Unfortunately, the so-called jazz stage had no financial support and very soon the musicians had to separate and were to meet, but from time to time at occasional concerts, chiefly at a yearly meeting at Krakow on All Souls Day that has since become a tradition.
Excuse me, why did it happen on All Souls Day?

Because it is a meeting of religion from old, for old generation and the young generation make, young generation of jazz in Poland make an idea, have an idea to make holiday for jazzmen in such kind of days because of blues atmosphere. And all generation in Krakow, in Poland, because Poland is very Catholic, they are afraid what this generation made of this holiday, 100% Catholic holiday, but they make it not official. So like sometimes some circles making something for clothes only, friends and so on. And, but it is a tradition up to date except last year when begin a new name for this simple jazz festival in Krakow. Because of public opinion that we must finish with this name, because we don't need to have enemies in citizens, what for and so on. And this clubs, organizer said, okay, main things for our, for us is to prolong this tradition through making the festivals the world.
And we don't have time left on the tape, so let's go ahead. Can we skip on to some more questions? Okay. When did your magazine get started?

In 56 February, so half a year before our October changes. I am proud of this date, because it was, can I say, frankly, it was like a hero indeed, you know. Nobody, nobody, nobody believed me that I can to prolong such kind of paper. Mm-hmm. Some people said to me, oh yes, one issue you can make maybe, if you find an editor. But next you can forget about it. It is impossible. You, you can understand what it is jazz in Poland.
Mm-hmm.

You can hear, but you cannot read in Polish. You, we must wait for a better times. And I started with my friend's help. I looked for a editor, of course, so-called editor in Artistic Club in Gdańsk. After my 12 months of activity in lectures about music and making like a jam session with live music and gramophone record sessions, I make this idea for an anniversary of this event and making this one issue. And then after four months, after terrible... How it is?
Say it in Polish.

Troubles. After terrible troubles, I make second, third and so on up to date. Now we have 13 years of... edition of jazz. We started from 5000 circulation. Now we have about 20,000. But the mystery, mystery of this 20,000 is that from beginning from four or five year, five years ago, ago, we started a special part in our paper, so-called rhythm and songs for teenagers, music lovers. And that is the reason that we, that our circulation is grown up to 20. Of course, if we had better possibilities, we can 50,000 also with help of publicity. But it is a state paper, state magazine, and they are... For state, it is enough that it is such kind of paper.
Yeah.

And it goes a little to another countries, and I hope that maybe next few years, maybe we can make much more circulations. Now is a little worse situation in jazz life in Poland. Worse than in rock and roll life.
Worse than in rock and roll life.
So if you know, want to have... if we have a little time to... Yeah, yeah.
Yeah, I...
Yes?
I wanted to ask you though, in listening to those records, I noticed the musicians play all... there are new tunes that I don't know. They don't play American tunes. Yes.

Beginning from maybe five or six years, maybe seven, several Polish musicians and groups making their own idea. Our musicians have begun to look for their own ways of expression. After using, by the long time, American originals and standards, from 1960, Polish musicians turned to their own musical tradition, and in particular to Polish folk music. They compose many jazz originals based on folk songs. I mean both of traditional and modern musicians and composers. And it gave, and today also in every concert, much more good impressions on white audience. Because they know very well American music and American tunes and originals and standards. And everybody are looking for something new. And it is paradox that we found a new things in repertory, I mean, we found a new things in old Polish folk tunes. Yes. It is not only in Poland, I know that in every country. And I must tell you that the great success for Polish jazz generation was the first visit of Willis Conover, who gave us maybe this idea to change a little our music.
Mm-hmm.
If you are interested, I can give you a few remarks about his first visit.
Yes, I would like to know about it.

No, it was probably eight or nine years ago, and we arranged a special concert in Philharmonic Hall in Warsaw. And Willis Conover came as a first time. He was very surprised by the grouse, versatility, and liveliness of the Polish jazz scene. At a large jazz concert in Philharmonic, giving thanks for an enthusiastic welcome, he said, It is I who should applaud you for the dignity that you have brought to the appreciation of jazz, and you, the musicians, for devoting your lies to music so far from its source, but to all of you musicians and observers for the warmth of the greeting you have given me here in Warsaw. and then said thanks. Now we have a little worse situation but because mostly musicians, jazz musicians cannot to live from jazz only, they are from various professions and professionalists goes mostly to another countries for job, for tournée one year, two years and we have in Poland only some groups that are in jazz clubs, students jazz clubs and from time to time at Philharmonic Hall.

Oh, one thing I notice about it, if you don't mind my saying this, is that I think you have a very good sense of humor as well as good rhythm in your playing. Those two things stand out to me. Mm-hmm. Ragtime also, I'd say. Tell me about the Polish sense of humor.

I think so that Polish young musicians likes very much traditional because of spirit, because of Polish, so-called Polish temperament. And I think so that it is very closely, closely connection between temperament of New Orleans, I mean music temperament, and Polish music, and so-called Polish music, Polkas and so on. It was in the past, it was in very good tempo. It's, it can say today Mazurkas, it swings. Mm-hmm. Yes.
Thank you.

And since first days of our movement, jazz movement, we have very, this traditional jazz is very popular. That is the reason that our young musicians, amateur musicians, has his, in every honor of every composer is to make own composition based on folk tune, folk tune, or something like that, because it's similar to various compositions born here in New Orleans. So thanks to God we can say so, that we have the opposite of modern group, and free jazz group, and third stream group, and laboratory group, so-called, we have some very good traditional group, like jazz band, from Krakow, from Krakow, Rectime jazz band Warsaw, old timer Warsaw, and bamboo today. Yes. We'll be here and we'll go. Yes, it is probably that it is only a few years and then shall come maybe in another shape. Shapes. The shapes, the things to come. But I must do, I have one more interesting thing. A special chapter in Polish jazz activities, connections of jazz composers with movies. Plenty of Polish motion pictures concern the music composed by Trzaskowski, Komeda, Kurilewicz, Matuszkiewicz, Milian. It is names of our popular musicians. For instance, Komeda is now in Hollywood. He makes a picture for Polanski, Rosemary babies in Paramount Studios. He has also plenty of contracts with in Sweden, Norway, Copenhagen and so on. And Polish music, film music is everyday popular. So we think so that it comes to white, white known that everybody in Europe and in America in the future maybe can know more about Polish music thanks to films. I'm sorry you don't
have more time. We're just about to run out of tape. You said you have to leave it too.

OK. So I want to thank you very much. We appreciate this. For me it is very nice to be here and I'm proud that you have not forget about me and of course I am of course a little old man but I hope that it is not to I am not a special optimist but I hope that maybe we shall see each other if not in New Orleans please I invite all of you to Warsaw to see something just justly interesting for you and please to remember very good that it is tapes the end yes because I should give address

segments.title: Sound check, date and introductions
segments.summary: Levels are tested, and the date (17 May 1968, New Orleans) and names are recorded.

segments.title: Birth in Warsaw, 1915
segments.summary: Balcerak says he was born in Warsaw on 7 March 1915.

segments.title: First contact with jazz at a film company office in Warsaw
segments.summary: His first job was at United Artists and London Films in Warsaw, where a colleague brought back jazz records and held jam sessions. He describes 1930s Polish jazz, English groups and record shops.

segments.title: Military service, wartime and the disguised German records
segments.summary: Military service from 1938 ended his listening. In 1944-45 he found German-labelled records in a house in Germany that turned out to be Benny Goodman jazz.

segments.chapter: Postwar Poland and jazz under Stalinism
segments.title: Navy magazine and Radio Gdansk after the war
segments.summary: He edited a Navy magazine, then from 1948 worked at Radio Gdansk, starting light music and jazz programs. He mentions YMCA clubs in Warsaw and Krakow.

segments.chapter: Postwar Poland and jazz under Stalinism
segments.title: Jazz banned as decadent Western music, 1948-52
segments.summary: Until Stalin's death, jazz was officially discouraged and survived only privately.

segments.chapter: Postwar Poland and jazz under Stalinism
segments.title: The thaw: Thiermann's concerts and the first Polish jazz stars
segments.summary: A read-aloud text describes jazz returning, concerts organised by Leopold Tiermann, a list of favourite Polish musicians, and the lack of financial support.

segments.chapter: Postwar Poland and jazz under Stalinism
segments.title: The All Souls Day jazz meeting in Krakow
segments.summary: He explains the Krakow tradition of a jazz gathering on All Souls Day and the Catholic sensitivities around it.

segments.title: Founding the magazine Jazz in 1956
segments.summary: He started the magazine Jazz in February 1956 against scepticism. Circulation grew from 5,000 to about 20,000, and it is a state magazine.

segments.title: Polish jazz turns to folk music
segments.summary: Since about 1960 Polish musicians have written originals based on folk songs instead of American standards.

segments.title: Willis Conover's first visit to Warsaw
segments.summary: He recalls Conover's first concert in the Warsaw Philharmonic Hall, and notes that Polish musicians often leave for work abroad.

segments.title: Polish temperament, traditional jazz bands and film composers
segments.summary: He links Polish temperament to New Orleans music and lists traditional bands (the transcript is garbled by an ASR loop). He ends with Polish jazz composers writing film music, including Komeda in Hollywood.

segments.title: Closing thanks and invitation to Warsaw
segments.summary: The tape runs out and Balcerak thanks the interviewers and invites them to Warsaw.
